+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 54.5
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The hum of the transfer vessel was a constant, low-frequency vibration that seemed to resonate directly in Arthur Neegan’s bones. It was a sound he knew well, the sound of machinery under load, but this was different. This was the sound of a journey not of his own choosing. He sat on a hard, molded bench that was more functional than comfortable, his hands resting on his knees. Across from him, two figures sat in identical stillness. Their armour was a matte, non-reflective black, devoid of any insignia save for a small, silver stylized starburst on the left breastplate—the emblem of the Antares diplomatic corps. They had not spoken a word since boarding. A small display screen on the wall cycled through various system diagnostics in green text, a constant, silent litany of pressure, oxygen, and velocity that did nothing to soothe Arthur’s nerves. He was an engineer; he understood the numbers. He knew the vessel was a standard Antares courier, a model prized for its reliability and speed, not its luxury. The fact that they had sent one for him, alone, was a statement in itself. He thought of his small hab-dome, the red dust perpetually coating the air-scrubber fins, the quiet satisfaction of a successful core sample. That life felt a lifetime away, shattered by the spectrographic analysis of a single, unassuming rock. His rock. The one that contained a purity of Azra that, according to the frantic, encrypted messages he’d intercepted before his ‘guests’ arrived, was theoretically impossible. It wasn’t a vein; it was a lode. A planetary-scale anomaly. The vessel’s deceleration was a gentle, firm push against his back. The green text on the screen shifted to a single word: *DOCKING*. A moment later, a soft chime confirmed the magnetic clamps had engaged. One of the armoured figures rose with a fluid grace that belied the bulk of the suit, and motioned with a gauntleted hand for Arthur to precede him. The airlock opened not onto a bustling spaceport, but into a quiet, private docking bay. It was sterile, lit by recessed panels in the ceiling that cast a soft, white light. The floor was a polished grey composite that reflected their images with perfect clarity. A man was waiting for them. He was older, perhaps in his seventh decade, with a face that was a roadmap of fine lines and a full head of silver hair meticulously combed. He wore a simple, high-collared tunic of dark blue material, cut in a style that felt archaic, yet carried an undeniable air of authority. He was unarmed. “Mr. Neegan,” he said, his voice a smooth, measured baritone. “I am Valerius. I apologize for the abruptness of your departure, but time is a resource nearly as valuable as Azra itself.” Arthur found his own voice, rough from disuse. “Where am I?” “You are aboard the *Concordance*, a private orbital station. Neutral territory, you might say. Please, walk with me.” Valerius turned and led the way from the docking bay, his steps unhurried. They moved down a corridor lined with dark wood paneling and polished brass fittings. It was like stepping into a museum, a stark contrast to the red dust and utilitarian plastic of Arthur’s life. A large viewport on their left showed the curve of Mars, a swirling ochre and white marble hanging in the black. “I’ve read your file, Mr. Neegan,” Valerius continued, not looking at him. “First-generation settler. Your parents were part of the Ares-7 expedition. A geologist and a hydroponic engineer. You followed in their footsteps, in a manner of speaking. Mining engineering. A practical, grounded profession. You appreciate the fundamental principles of things.” “I appreciate a good rock when I see one,” Arthur replied, his engineer’s mind trying to deconstruct the man, the station, the situation. “Indeed. And you have found the best rock in the known galaxy.” Valerius stopped before a set of heavy, carved doors, which slid soundlessly open to reveal a spacious study. More wood, more brass. A large oak desk dominated the room, and behind it, another viewport, this one looking out towards the distant, pinprick stars. He gestured for Arthur to sit in a comfortable leather chair opposite the desk. “Let us dispense with the pleasantries, Mr. Neegan. I represent a consortium of interests that predates the Martian Colonial Authority and the Outer Belt Corporations. We are historians, in a way. We study the long arc of humanity. And right now, that arc is bending towards a precipice.” He steepled his fingers. “Azra is the fulcrum. The corporations see it as a fuel for a new generation of warships. The governments see it as a means to project power. They are all children, squabbling over a torch that will burn their house down. They see its use in accelerating decay. They see a weapon. They do not see the truth.” Arthur leaned forward. “And what is the truth?” “The truth,” Valerius said, his eyes gleaming, “is that controlled decay is the key to controlled *stability*. It is the foundation for a true interstellar society, not just a series of frantic, one-way jumps. It is the key to terraforming, to stabilizing stellar outputs, to extending the lifespan of suns. But that potential requires a guiding hand, not a greedy fist.” He leaned back, his posture relaxed but his gaze intense. “Your claim sits atop the single largest, purest deposit of Azra ever discovered. To let the corporations or the colonial government have it would be to hand a loaded weapon to a child. We cannot allow that.” “So you’re just going to take it?” Arthur asked, a familiar cold anger starting to bubble. Valerius smiled faintly. “No. That would be crude. It would also violate a dozen treaties and create a political firestorm we would rather avoid. Instead, we are offering you a partnership, Mr. Neegan. You will retain legal title to your claim. You will be appointed as our chief on-site engineering consultant. You will oversee the extraction process. In return, you will receive a percentage of the refined Azra so vast that the concept of wealth will become meaningless to you. More importantly, you will have our protection. And you will have the knowledge that your discovery is being used to secure humanity’s future, not to hasten its end.” He slid a thin, metallic slate across the desk. “The full terms are on here. The alternative, I’m afraid, is less appealing. The corporations are not as… diplomatic as we are. They will arrive soon. They will not offer you a partnership. They will take your land, your research, and likely your life, and they will use your discovery to build weapons that will make the last war look like a border skirmish.” Arthur looked from the slate to Valerius’s calm, patient face. He was a mining engineer, a man who dealt with geology and physics. Now he was caught in a geology of power, the tectonic plates of empires shifting around his small, unassuming plot of Martian land. “Why me?” he asked, the question finally feeling real. “Because you are a man who understands foundations,” Valerius said softly. “And we need a man who can help us build a new one.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter competently executes the brief: Arthur is aboard the transfer vessel, meets a mysterious off-world party (Valerius), receives an offer, and the scene is dialogue-heavy with world-building hints of corporate/government intrigue. The Asimovian flavor is attempted through the "big picture" exposition about Azra's potential for controlled stability versus weaponization, and the retrofuturistic wood-and-brass station aesthetic is a nice touch evoking classic sci-fi's anachronistic futures. Strengths: The prose is clean and controlled, with good pacing between description and dialogue. Valerius is suitably ambiguous—a "diplomatic" threat wrapped in courtesy. The offer's structure (partnership vs. implied coercion) creates genuine stakes. The "geology of power" metaphor tying Arthur's profession to his predicament is a well-earned thematic touch. Weaknesses: The piece is competent rather than inspired. Valerius is a fairly stock "wise manipulator" archetype; his dialogue occasionally slips into pure exposition ("We are historians, in a way. We study the long arc of humanity") that tells rather than dramatizes. Arthur is largely passive—he asks three short questions and receives lectures. The intrigue hints are somewhat generic (shadowy consortium, treaties, "the last war") without specific, surprising detail. The prose occasionally overreaches ("a roadmap of fine lines," "eyes gleaming"). The ending line is neat but borders on pat. Dialogue is serviceable but rarely crackles; Valerius does most of the talking and Arthur's voice is underdeveloped. There's little emotional complexity—Arthur's fear and anger are stated rather than deeply felt. Still, it's coherent, on-brief, and readable, with no major tonal missteps. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 61.8
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom smells like secrets. It’s a sharp, metallic cocktail of fixer and developer that clings to the back of your throat, a scent I’ve come to associate with revelation. Under the crimson glow of the safelight, the world is stripped down to essentials: shadows, the soft clink of glass, the steady gurgle of the running water bath. And Elliot. He’s six years younger than me, a fact that feels ludicrously irrelevant in this blood-washed space. Here, he’s the one with the steady hand. I watch him fish a sheet of photographic paper from the developer bath with a pair of tongs, his movements precise and economical. His thrift-shop-nu-goth aesthetic, which usually reads as a carefully constructed statement, feels like a second skin in the dim light. The ripped black band t-shirt hangs off one pale shoulder, and a silver ankh rests in the hollow of his collarbone. I’ve spent a semester admiring the whole package from my usual vantage point: a distance I controlled. I’m Dani. I don’t do pining. I see, I appreciate, I acquire. My relationships have a clear, satisfying arc. But with Elliot, it’s been different. I’ve been… observing. Fascinated by the dissonance of him: the heavy boots and chains contrasted with a voice so soft you have to lean in to catch it, the intimidating intellect that emerges in class critiques delivered with a quiet, almost shy, confidence. He’s a study in beautiful contradictions. “We’re losing the highlights,” he murmurs, his gaze fixed on the ghostly image forming in the tray. He’s right. I got the exposure wrong, my usual assertiveness blunted by the late hour and his proximity. “Right. Shit.” I reach for the tongs, but he’s already moving the print to the stop bath. The acetic bite of the chemical fills the air between us. We’ve been at this for three nights in a row, our final project on ‘Perceived Identity’ demanding more of us than either of us anticipated. The irony isn’t lost on me. He works in silence for a while, the only sounds the slosh of liquids and the low hum of the ventilation fan. It’s a comfortable quiet, the kind that settles in your bones. Then, he speaks, so quietly I almost mistake it for a thought. “Sometimes I wonder if the camera is lying.” I look over at him. He’s not looking at me, but at a stack of blank photographic paper. “How so?” “It just shows what’s there. The surface. But what if… what if the surface is the wrong part?” He finally turns, and in the red light, his eyes look huge and dark, fathomless. “Like, it captures the shell, but not the… not the thing inside trying to get out.” My heart does a strange, slow-motion flip. This is it. The unspoken thing that’s been simmering between us, denser than the chemical fog. My first instinct, my Dani-instinct, is to take charge. To step in, put a hand on his arm, and say, *It’s okay, whatever it is, I’m here. Tell me everything.* To create a safe space by commandeering it. But I stop myself. That’s not what he needs. That’s not what *this* is. I see the tremor in his lower lip, the raw nerve he’s just exposed. My usual desire to lead is crushed by a newer, more powerful urge: to protect this moment, to give him the room to exist in it. I lean back against the counter, giving him space. “The surface is just the starting point, though, right? The rest is interpretation.” He seems to consider this, a small line appearing between his brows. “I’ve been… questioning things,” he says, the words barely audible. “Not just who I am, but… what I am. Gender-wise.” He says it fast, like ripping off a bandage, and then immediately looks away as if the confession has burned him. And there it is. The thing that reconfigures my entire understanding of him, and of my own attraction. I’ve always been drawn to strong lines, to defined presentations. Butch women, femme men, people who wore their identities like beautifully tailored suits. Elliot was always a bit of a blur, and I realize now that’s what I’ve been chasing. The mystery. My attraction doesn’t vanish. If anything, it intensifies, sharpening into something new and dizzyingly complex. It’s no longer just about his style or his intellect. It’s about this. The courage of this. The privilege of witnessing the moment he begins to dismantle his own shell. I feel a fierce, protective surge, but it’s tangled with a thrilling, almost voyeuristic excitement. I’m here at the ground floor of someone becoming. I don’t know what to say. Anything feels like too much. So I just nod, and wait. He starts to hum. It’s a soft, tuneless melody, almost a lullaby. He does it while he waits for the next print to reveal itself in the developer, his gaze distant, lost in thought. The sound is so vulnerable, so unselfconscious, it wraps around my heart. In the red, intimate dark, it feels like a prayer. It’s an offering more honest than any words. I stop thinking about taking charge. I stop analyzing my own identity, my own labels. For the first time in a long time, I’m just… present. I’m watching the image slowly bleach into existence in the chemical bath—ghostly trees, a path leading nowhere. And I’m listening to Elliot hum. The two things weave together, a new kind of art being created right here in this small, secret room. He stops humming, the silence feeling suddenly profound. He glances at me, a flicker of apprehension in his eyes. I give him the smallest, gentlest smile I can muster. “I like that tune,” I say, my voice softer than I’ve ever heard it. He relaxes, just a fraction. “It’s nothing.” “It’s not nothing,” I say, and I mean it. Nothing about this is nothing. I don’t know where this is going, what this makes me, or what he will decide to be. But for the first time, I realize that not knowing isn’t a problem to be solved. It’s a negative, waiting to be exposed. And I am more than ready to see what develops.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, controlled piece that fulfills nearly all prompt requirements. The darkroom setting is used as an extended metaphor (negatives, exposure, development) without becoming heavy-handed—mostly. The red-light confessional atmosphere is well established through sensory detail: chemical smells, tongs, developer baths, the hum of the ventilation fan. Dani's voice is consistent and distinct: clipped, self-aware, assertive in narration even when she withholds assertiveness in action. The central conflict—Dani's instinct to "commandeer" a safe space versus her choice to give Elliot room—is dramatized rather than merely stated, though the story does lean on internal monologue to explain it. The gender-questioning confession is handled with restraint; Elliot "rips off the bandage" and retreats, which feels true to a shy 19-year-old. The humming beat is the piece's best moment—an offering "more honest than any words"—genuine show-don't-show. Weaknesses: the ending's metaphor ("It's a negative, waiting to be exposed... see what develops") is clever but borders on tidy and cute, a slight incongruous uplift for a moment that had been pitched as uncertainty. Some lines are over-explained ("I feel a fierce, protective surge, but it's tangled with a thrilling, almost voyeuristic excitement")—telling the reader the exact emotional recipe rather than letting it emerge. Dani's self-characterization ("I'm Dani. I don't do pining. I see, I appreciate, I acquire") is efficient but a touch on-the-nose. The dialogue is minimal and functional rather than memorable; "Sometimes I wonder if the camera is lying" is a serviceable but slightly predictable confessional device. The word count lands near the 1000-word target. The chemistry is understated and tender, appropriately awkward, though the "unexpected chemistry" is more implied than developed—Elliot remains somewhat opaque, which is arguably the point but also limits his characterization. Overall: competent, sensitive, well-crafted literary fiction with a few over-explained passages and a slightly too-neat closing metaphor. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 56.6
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The roar of the scooter was a beast unleashed upon the cobblestones, a sound that belonged to the city’s chaotic heart. Ben, head buried in a guidebook titled *A Scholar’s Rome*, was a stationary island in a rushing river. He didn’t hear the beast until it was upon him, its horn blaring a staccato of pure Italian indignation. He stumbled back, the book flying from his hands as a flash of red metal screeched to a halt inches from his knees. “Ma che vuoi? Sordo?” The voice was sharp, musical, and furious. “You walk with your head in a book in the middle of the street? You want to die with a footnote?” Ben looked up, his heart hammering against his ribs. The rider was a woman, straddling a Ducati like she was born to it. She pulled off her helmet, shaking out a mane of dark, espresso-coloured hair. Her eyes, the colour of rich honey, blazed at him. “I’m so terribly sorry,” he stammered, fumbling for his Italian. “Mi dispiace. Molto. I was… distracted.” Alessandra—though he didn’t know her name yet—watched him, his flustered apology, his tortoise-shell glasses askew. The anger in her face dissolved into a smirk, a flicker of pure, unadulterated mischief. “Distracted,” she repeated, the English word tasting like a foreign fruit. “You are distracted in Roma. That is like being sleepy at a fireworks display.” She kicked the stand of her bike and dismounted, all leather and fluid grace. She bent to retrieve his book, her fingers tracing the gold-leaf title. “A Scholar’s Rome,” she read, her voice dripping with theatrical pity. “You will not find my Rome in here.” “I… I beg your pardon?” She looked at him, a long, appraising glance that made him feel simultaneously scrutinized and seen. “My name is Alessandra. You have nearly caused my premature death. The least you can do is let me buy you a coffee. An apology coffee. For scaring me.” Ben, a man whose life was a series of scheduled appointments and footnotes, found himself nodding. “Alright. Yes. Thank you. I’m Ben.” “Ben,” she said, testing the name. “Simple. Like a doorbell. Come.” She didn’t lead him to a tourist café. She guided him through a labyrinth of narrow alleys to a tiny hole-in-the-wall, the air thick with the scent of roasted beans and sugar. As they sat at a minuscule table, her hand moved with a dancer’s swiftness, a quick, darting motion under the table. He didn’t see what she took, only the satisfied, clandestine smile that touched her lips. A small, ceramic salt shaker from the neighbouring empty table vanished into her jacket pocket. “You are a courier?” he asked, trying to make conversation over the din. “Sì. A messenger. I deliver important things. Secrets. Documents. The occasional cannoli.” She leaned forward, her voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. “I know this city’s secrets, Ben. The real ones. Not the dates on old statues.” An impulse, wild and undeniable, sparked in her eyes. “Finish your coffee. I am giving you a real tour.” Before he could protest, she was pulling him back out into the street, tossing him the spare helmet from her scooter. “Hold on,” she commanded, and the world dissolved into a blur of motion, wind, and the intoxicating scent of her leather jacket. He clung to her waist, a clumsy anchor to her wild storm, as they weaved through traffic that defied all logic. She took him everywhere and nowhere. To a hidden courtyard where a lone orange tree grew, its fruit heavy and fragrant. To the roof of an apartment building, accessed via a rickety fire escape she swore was a ‘secret imperial passage’. They sat, legs dangling over the edge, above the sea of terracotta tiles. “You’re mad,” Ben said, but he was laughing, the sound foreign and exhilarating to his own ears. “Mad is boring,” she retorted. “I am interesting.” Later, in the bustling chaos of Campo de' Fiori market, a man with a weathered face and ink-stained fingers grabbed her arm. “Alessandra. Still causing trouble?” “Marco,” she purred, untangling herself. “Always a pleasure.” Marco’s eyes, dark and knowing, flicked to Ben. “You be careful with this one, *amico*,” he said in surprisingly good English. “She collects things. Moments. And sometimes… things that are not hers.” Ben frowned, confused, but Alessandra just laughed, a bright, dismissive sound. “Pay him no mind. He is just jealous he’s no longer one of my exhibits.” She dragged Ben away, but Marco’s words echoed in his mind. He started noticing things—the way her eyes would linger on a shiny trinket, the subtle dip of her fingers into an open market stall, the small, smooth stone she’d slipped from a fountain’s edge and now palmed in her hand. She was a whirlwind of curated chaos, and he was utterly captivated. As dusk painted the sky in shades of apricot and violet, she brought him to Gianicolo Hill. The city spread out below them, a glittering carpet of lights. The wind had gentled, and the air was still. The manic energy of the day had softened into something else, something charged and intimate. “Marco was right, you know,” she said quietly, her gaze fixed on the horizon. Ben’s breath caught. “I do take things.” She turned to him, her honey-coloured eyes serious for the first time all day. From her pocket, she pulled out a small, ornate silver key. It glinted in the fading light. “I stole this this morning,” she confessed, her voice barely a whisper. “From a locked cabinet in a church near the Trevi Fountain. I don’t know what it opens. Maybe a confessional. Maybe a box of old hymns. Maybe nothing at all.” She took his hand, her fingers cool against his skin, and pressed the key into his palm. It was heavy, solid. Real. “A souvenir,” she said, a ghost of her earlier smirk returning. “Of your stolen day.” He looked from the key in his hand to her face, a beautiful, enigmatic mask in the twilight. He wanted to ask what it meant, if he’d see her again, if this was all a game. But before he could speak, she pulled on her helmet, gave him a final, inscrutable look, and kick-started her Ducati. The engine roared to life, and with a small, defiant wave, she was gone—a red phantom disappearing into the Roman night. Ben stood alone, the wind whipping at his coat, the stolen key clutched in his fist. He was miles from his rented apartment, his guidebook was lost, and his carefully planned sabbatical was officially, gloriously, derailed. He had never felt more alive.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, well-structured romance vignette that hits the prompt's beats: near-collision at Trevi, culture clash, the unsanctioned tour, subtle kleptomania hints, and a bittersweet parting with a symbolic stolen key. The prose is generally clean and evocative, with some nice lines ("You want to die with a footnote?", "Simple. Like a doorbell."). The kleptomania is handled with reasonable subtlety—salt shaker, market stall, fountain stone—though Marco's exposition ("She collects things... things that are not hers") flattens the subtext into explicit telling, which slightly undermines the prompt's request that it not be explicitly revealed. Alessandra's direct confession at the end also trades mystery for sentimentality. Weaknesses: the characters are somewhat stock (fiery Italian woman, bumbling British academic), and the "transformation" of Ben from cautious to exhilarated is asserted more than earned through specific escalating choices—he mostly gets dragged along. The ending leans romantic and uplifting ("never felt more alive") which is appropriate to the genre, though the emotional payoff arrives quickly. Some imagery is pleasant but occasionally clichéd (espresso-coloured hair, honey eyes, terracotta tiles, apricot and violet dusk). Dialogue is serviceable and characterful but occasionally on-the-nose. The word count is roughly appropriate; the scene structure is coherent and paced well. Overall this is solid, professional-grade commercial romance writing with no major structural failures, but limited originality or emotional depth beyond genre conventions. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 56.3
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The low thrum of the station’s gravity plating is a heartbeat, a constant, reassuring rhythm beneath my feet. It’s the sound of home. I wipe the same spot on the bar counter, a worn, dark patch of wood that’s seen more spilled secrets than spilled liquor. The rag is damp, smelling faintly of sanitizing fluid and the Vega whisky I sloshed earlier. The motion is a meditation, a way to center myself in the gentle chaos of the Last Outpost. “…and the port stabilizer on the *Rock-Hopper* is shot again,” Joric grumbles from his usual stool. His face is a roadmap of old mining accidents, but his eyes are soft. “Third rotation this cycle. I tell you, Nets, the corp is using cheaper and cheaper parts.” I nod, keeping my eyes on the bar. “You want me to have a word with Kaelen when he brings his next shipment in? He can probably get you a military-grade one off the books.” Joric snorts into his synth-ale. “And have my ship impounded for possessing contraband? No, thank you. I’ll just bitch about it. Cheaper.” From a shadowed corner booth, Elara, a trader in rare textiles, lowers her data-slate. Her voice is as smooth and cool as the silk she deals in. “Bitching is a currency here, Joric. Just don’t expect it to buy you a new stabilizer.” “It buys me another drink,” he retorts, raising his glass to her. “And on that note,” I say, tossing the rag onto the counter, “can I get you two anything else, or are you just going to verbally re-calibrate the station’s power grid for me?” “Another ale,” Joric says. “And a word of advice. Don’t get old.” “I’ll try to remember that.” I turn to grab a clean glass, the familiar clink and clatter of my bar my favorite symphony. That’s when the door hisses open. The change is subtle, at first. The ambient chatter dips by a few decibels. A few heads turn. I straighten up, wiping my hands on my apron. The newcomer stands in the doorway, a silhouette against the brighter corridor light. Then they step inside, and the hush becomes more pronounced. It’s a Xylos. We don’t get many of them out this far. They’re usually found charting nebulae or tending to the great archives on Core worlds. This one is a mess. Their species is known for its serene, almost meditative stillness, but this one… they’re vibrating with a frantic energy. Their long, tentacle-like dreads, usually woven with beads and tiny, chiming sensors, are askew. One is twitching, tapping a nervous rhythm against their thigh. They move with a jerky, unnatural gait, their multi-faceted eyes scanning the room like they’re expecting a threat to leap out from the shadows. They bypass the empty tables and make a beeline for my bar, plopping down onto a stool three down from Joric. Their voice, when it comes, is a dry rasp, completely devoid of the melodic lilt I’ve heard in recordings. “Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double.” I raise an eyebrow but keep my expression neutral. It’s my job. “Rough day?” “You have no idea.” They don’t look at me, instead staring at the rows of bottles behind me as if they hold the answers to the universe. I grab the Vega, a dark, smoky liquor that burns all the way down. I pour a generous double, the amber liquid glugging into the heavy glass. I slide it over. The Xylos’s hand, with its too-many joints, trembles slightly as they wrap their fingers around it. They down half of it in one go, their whole body shuddering. I pick up my rag and resume wiping the same spot on the counter. The rhythm is off now. It’s less meditative, more of a nervous tic. “That bad, huh?” They finally look at me, and I see it in their eyes. It’s not just stress; it’s terror. A deep, soul-shaking fear. “They found me.” My hand stills on the bar. “Who’s ‘they’?” The Xylos glances around the room. Joric is pretending not to listen, but I can see the tension in his shoulders. Elara has put her data-slate down again, her full attention on us. The newcomer seems to realize this is not the place for specifics. They lower their voice. “People who want what’s mine.” “This is the Outpost,” I say softly, leaning forward a little. “Nothing leaves this bar unless you want it to. It’s kind of our whole thing.” A bitter, broken sound escapes their mouth, maybe meant to be a laugh. “It’s not just a thing, bartender. It’s a life’s work. Twenty cycles. Mapping the Veil of Echoes. Charting the ghost-stars.” They take another shuddering swallow of the whisky. “My charts. They’re not just data. They’re… they’re songs. The music of creation.” Joric grunts. “Corp steal your research? Happens.” “Worse,” the Xylos whispers, and the sound is so full of pain it makes my chest ache. They finish their drink and push the glass toward me for a refill. I oblige, my movements slow and deliberate. “The Silicate Collective. They don’t just want the charts.” I wipe the bar. The wood is starting to feel damp under my hand. “What do they want, then?” Their eyes, faceted and complex, lock onto mine. All the frantic energy is gone, replaced by a chilling, hollow dread. “They don’t just want the charts, Nets. They want to unmake me. Erase the singer, so they can claim the song for themselves.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece adheres well to the prompt: first person, present tense, cozy sci-fi bar setting, roughly 60% dialogue, conflict introduced (the Xylos pursued by the Silicate Collective) and left unresolved. The bartender's voice is consistent — observant, wry, protective of her space. The regulars (Joric, Elara) are lightly but efficiently sketched, giving the bar a lived-in feel. Strengths: the opening sensory grounding (gravity plating hum, worn bar wood), the gradual shift in atmosphere when the stranger enters, and the escalation of stakes through dialogue rather than exposition dumps. The "songs of creation" / "erase the singer" conceit gives the threat a poetic, alien flavor appropriate to the genre. Weaknesses: the ending is marred by an obvious repetition — the Xylos says "They don't just want the charts" twice, first as a cliffhanger and then again verbatim, which reads like a drafting error and deflates the final line's impact. Some elements are stock: the grizzled miner, the mysterious past bartender, the "you have no idea" exchange. The stranger's terror is somewhat told rather than shown in places ("It's not just stress; it's terror"). The "Silicate Collective" and "Veil of Echoes" are serviceable but generic sci-fi names. Minor logic slip: the stranger calls her "Nets" before being told her name (though the prompt implies regulars use it, a stranger wouldn't know it — a small believability flaw). Prose is clean and flows well without becoming purple; imagery is adequate though not exceptional. Emotionally engaging but not deeply complex — the fear is vivid, but Nets's own past is only hinted at. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 74.1
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The diesel fumes hang in the air, a ghost of the truck that just kicked me to the curb. Downtown New Orleans. It doesn’t look like anywhere I’ve ever been, not even on TV. It’s louder, for one thing. A trumpet wails somewhere, lonely and hopeful all at once, and the sound of it gets tangled up with the rumble of a streetcar and a hundred different conversations spilling out of doorways. The air is thick enough to chew, hot and wet like a breath in your face, and it smells of river water, fried dough, and something sweet and rotting underneath. The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder. I hitch it back up, the weight of my entire life—three t-shirts, two pairs of jeans, a toothbrush, and ninety-seven dollars in cash—pulling me off balance. I feel like a fraud. Like someone will point and shout, ‘Hey, that one doesn’t belong!’ But no one even looks at me. I am invisible. For the first hour, I just walk. My feet, shoved into worn-out sneakers, start to ache on the uneven cobblestones. I passed a cathedral with spires that stab the grey sky, and now I’m standing in front of a park, Jackson Square, a sign says. Iron-laced balconies surround it, painted in colours of a bruised sunset. Street performers are setting up: a man on a stool with a guitar, a woman painted silver who stands perfectly still. This is the drama I used to invent back home, but this is real. It’s happening all around me, and I’m just standing here like an idiot, the backpack strap slipping again. My stomach growls, a loud, embarrassing complaint. Dad’s voice echoes in my head, sharp as broken glass. *This is a choice you’re making, Taylor. A selfish, destructive choice.* The memory is a punch to the gut, stealing the little air the humidity left me. Mom crying. The slam of my bedroom door. The sheer, stupid panic that had me stuffing my backpack and climbing out my window at two in the morning. It wasn’t a choice. It was… survival. I think. I sink onto a bench, the paint peeling and sticking to my jeans. I let the backpack strap fall this time. I can’t hold it up anymore. I rest my head in my hands, and for a second, the urge to just sit here and cry is so overwhelming my shoulders shake. But I don’t. Crying is for when you have a place to cry. Right now, I just have a bench. “You look like you’re about to get swallowed by the pavement.” I jump, my head snapping up. A kid is leaning against the arm of the bench on the other end, not looking at me, but at the silver statue-woman. He can’t be much older than me. Maybe seventeen? He’s got a shock of dark hair that falls into his eyes, and he’s wearing a hoodie despite the heat, the sleeves pushed up to his elbows. There’s a smudge of charcoal on his cheek. “What?” I manage, my voice hoarse. “The pavement,” he says, turning his head. His eyes are a pale, washed-out blue. “It’s got a taste for runaways. You gotta watch it.” He gestures with his chin towards my backpack. “That all you got?” The question is so direct it catches me off guard. My defenses flare up. “None of your business.” He holds up his hands, a mock surrender. “Easy, tiger. Just making conversation. Name’s Jinx.” “Taylor.” The name feels weird in my mouth, still new and unfamiliar. “Alright, Taylor. You new here? I mean, *new* new.” I nod, not trusting myself to speak. My heart is doing this stupid, frantic tap dance against my ribs. He knows. How does he know? Jinx smirks, but it’s not a mean smirk. It’s tired. “It’s the look. The way you’re staring at everything like it might bite you, and the way you’re trying not to stare at people like you’re afraid they might. Plus, you’re sitting on the prime real estate for the after-dark crowd. You move on by sundown, you hear me?” “Why?” I ask, my voice barely a whisper. “Let’s just say the glitter gets a little gritty at night. This place belongs to different people then.” He pushes off the bench and stands, stretching. “You hungry?” My traitorous stomach growls again, loud enough for him to hear. I flush, heat crawling up my neck. Jinx just nods. “Come on. I know a spot.” Every instinct I have is screaming *no*. The school counsellor’s voice about ‘poor impulse control’ is ringing in my ears. But my stomach is louder. And he’s right. I am completely, utterly out of my depth. I follow him, a few steps behind, the backpack finally settled in the crook of my arm. He doesn’t try to make small talk. He just weaves through the crowds with an easy confidence I am faking so hard it hurts. We end up near the river, where the smells are stronger and the tourists thinner. He ducks into an alleyway, and my panic spikes again. This is it. This is how it happens. But he just stops by a dumpster behind a restaurant and pulls a half-full bag of beignets from the top of a trash can. They’re in a paper bag, barely touched. “Stale,” he says, handing them to me. “But it’s food. Don’t think about where it’s been.” I take one. The powdered sugar gets all over my fingers. It’s a little tough, but it’s sweet and warm from the sun, and it’s the best thing I’ve ever tasted. I devour two before I even breathe. Jinx watches me, leaning against the brick wall. He doesn’t take any for himself. “Aren’t you eating?” I ask, my mouth full. “Already ate,” he says, but his eyes flicker down to the bag. A lie. I’ve gotten good at spotting those lately. “So, what’s your story? Family sucks? Boyfriend sucks?” “Something like that,” I say, wiping my mouth. I don’t know if I can say the words. *My dad thinks I’m a pervert and my mom wishes I was still her little girl.* Not exactly a charming icebreaker. He nods like he understands everything. “Yeah. Something like that. It’s always something like that.” The sun is beginning to set, painting the sky in shades of orange and purple. The music from the French Quarter seems to get louder, wilder. The city is waking up for the night. Jinx is right; the vibe is shifting. I feel a prickle on the back of my neck. “You got a place to stay?” he asks, his voice low. I just shake my head. My throat feels tight. The adrenaline from this morning is gone, replaced by a deep, bone-weary dread. He looks at me for a long moment, his pale eyes unreadable. Then he sighs, a sound that seems to carry the weight of a hundred bad nights. “Alright. Come on. There’s a spot I know. It’s not great, but it’s dry.” He pushes off the wall. “But Taylor?” “Yeah?” “Don’t trust anyone. Not even me.” He turns and walks deeper into the alley, disappearing into the growing shadows. I stand there for a second, the last beignet clutched in my hand. The strap on my backpack slips off my shoulder, but this time I don’t bother to pick it up. I just take a breath, tasting sugar and river water and fear, and I follow him into the dark.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This chapter competently executes the brief: first-person, mixed tense, Taylor's voice, a first day in New Orleans, a fellow runaway with hinted secrets, and internal monologue threaded with conflict. The strongest element is the sensory grounding of the city — the trumpet, the chewable humidity, the "sweet and rotting" undertone — which does real atmospheric work rather than decorating. Taylor's voice is consistent and age-appropriate, with a self-deprecating wit ("Crying is for when you have a place to cry. Right now, I just have a bench") that earns sympathy without wallowing. Jinx is serviceable but familiar: the streetwise, world-weary mentor figure with the quirky name and the "don't trust anyone, not even me" exit line is a well-worn archetype. The character is given a few good details (the lie about having eaten, the charcoal smudge, the hoodie in the heat), but the "issues and secrets" are gestured at rather than developed — acceptable for a first chapter, though the beats are predictable. The dumpster beignets scene is the chapter's best moment: it shows Jinx's competence and Taylor's desperation concretely, and the spotted lie adds texture. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally reaches for stock similes ("sharp as broken glass," "a punch to the gut," "heart doing a stupid tap dance") that flatten otherwise sharp writing. The pacing is well-controlled, but the ending's "follow him into the dark" beat is exactly what the reader expects. Some emotional beats are told rather than shown ("My defenses flare up," "my panic spikes"). The parents' rejection is rendered in efficient shorthand, but the flashback material is more summarized than dramatized. Overall this is solid, professional YA writing with a believable protagonist, decent dialogue, and genuine atmosphere — above average, but not transcendent. It plays safe within its genre's conventions. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 68.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Midas stared at the map, which wasn’t a map so much as a stained placemat from a long-dead pizza franchise. He’d drawn on it with a piece of charcoal. The X marked their objective. The X was always the problem. “Right,” he said, to the room at large and the small, fuzzy koala perched on a stack of encyclopaedias. “The Temple of Mart. Electronics aisle, third shelf from the top, behind the defunct display of ‘Smart’ Toasters. That’s where the C-cells will be.” Chewy, a relic of a forgotten era when children demanded toys that could talk and therefore inevitably held conversations more interesting than their owners, remained silent. His glass eyes stared into the middle distance, a stoic observer of the fall of man. Midas prodded him. “Any thoughts? Words of wisdom? A jingle for a car that hasn’t existed in fifty years?” The koala’s head twitched. A low, mechanical gargle emanated from his fuzzy stomach. Then, in a cheerful, pre-recorded voice that was far too loud for the dusty silence of the library, he announced, “*Got milk?*” “No,” Midas sighed. “And we’re not likely to. The dairy herds are fiercely territorial and you, my friend, are running on your last dregs of power. Soon you’ll be just a very plush, very quiet paperweight. And that’s why we’re doing this.” Their home base was the central branch of the city library, a fortress of paper and concrete that had survived the Ruin¹ mostly intact. It was a good place to live, if you liked the smell of decaying paper and the constant, looming threat of mildew. Today, however, the mission required them to leave this sanctuary and venture into the Concrete Savannah, a place where the feral shopping trolleys roamed. The journey to the Temple of Mart² was uneventful, which Midas knew was just the universe lulling him into a false sense of security. The trouble started, as it always did, when they got there. The Temple’s automatic doors, of course, no longer opened automatically. They were jammed half-open, a gaping maw that smelled of dust and desperation. And, as was so often the case with places of former commerce, it had been claimed. A figure emerged from the gloom. He was wearing a tattered blue vest over a collection of rags and had a barcode tattooed on his forehead. A member of the Cult of the Checkout. “Halt,” the man said, his voice hollow. “You stand before the sacred aisles. What is your purpose?” Midas held up his hands, a universal gesture for ‘I am not heavily armed and just want some batteries.’ “We’re on a simple pilgrimage. We seek the Powered Cells of C. For… ritual purposes.” The cultist’s eyes narrowed. “All items must be scanned. Do you have a loyalty card?” “Ah. No. It, uh, perished in the Great Data Wipe.” “A technicality,” the cultist sneered. “The price must be paid. In tribute. Or in blood.” It was at this precise moment that Chewy, jostled in Midas’s satchel, chose to awaken. “*I’m lovin’ it!*” he chirped, his voice echoing in the cavernous space. The cultist froze. His eyes went wide. A sound like a rattling breath came from his throat. “The… the Slogan of the Founder…” Midas didn’t wait for theological debate. He ducked past the man and sprinted into the maze of fallen shelves. The cultist’s shout of “Heretic! Un-scanned item!” followed him, but was soon drowned out by a deeper, more guttural sound from the rear of the store. A low growl that spoke of territorial disputes and a very poor attitude towards trespassers. The Guardian.³ Midas found the electronics aisle, a disaster zone of cracked screens and snarled cables. He spied them: a blister pack of four, glorious C-cells, hanging on a peg. He grabbed them, a triumphant surge in his chest. He’d done it. He’d beaten the odds. He turned to make a hasty retreat and ran face-first into a wall of fur and muscle. The Guardian was not, as rumour suggested, a mutated security drone. It was, in fact, a monstrously large badger that had somehow made its nest in a pile of discounted yoga mats. It was not happy. “Okay,” Midas said, backing away slowly. “Easy now. No need to get… aggressive.” The badger, which Midas would later mentally dub the ‘Price-Check Badger’, snorted a cloud of dust and charged. Panic is a wonderful motivator. Midas’s survival instincts, which usually manifested as ‘find a slightly less dangerous place to be’, kicked into overdrive. He dove into a nearby shopping trolley, kicking off from a shelf and sending the metal cage careening down the main thoroughfare. Chewy bounced on his lap. “*Every kiss begins with Kay!*” the koala offered helpfully. The trolley gained speed, a silver missile of consumerist salvation. It swerved, it skidded, it ploughed through a display of beanbags. Midas held on for dear life as the badger gave chase, its angry snarls receding as they shot out of the half-open doors and into the street. He arrived back at the library an hour later, pushing the mangled trolley. He had lost a shoe, gained a spectacular bruise on his forehead, and was pretty sure he’d pulled something important in his back. But in his hand, he clutched the blister pack of C-cells. He slumped into his chair, prised the batteries free with his teeth, and popped them into Chewy’s compartment. The koala’s eyes flickered to life. His head swivelled. He looked at Midas, a beacon of successful endeavour, a testament to human resilience against all odds. Then he opened his mouth and chirped, in the most infuriatingly cheerful tone imaginable, “*Melts in your mouth, not in your hand!*” Midas closed his eyes. Tomorrow, he thought, he’d just stay home. Tomorrow would probably be worse. *** ¹ The Ruin wasn’t a single event, like a bang or a whimper. It was more of a long, drawn-out process of things stopping. The internet went first, followed by logistics, then power, and finally, the collective will to pretend to know what a QR code was for. ² The Big Box stores, with their vast, cavernous interiors and towering shelves of useless junk, were considered the modern-day equivalents of ancient tombs. They were full of treasure, but also booby-traps with collapsing shelves and, occasionally, things that had nested in the bedding department and developed a taste for human flesh. ³ Guardians were a common feature of the more promising scavenging sites. They could be anything from a territorial pack of feral dogs to a particularly aggressive sentient mold. The rule of thumb was: if it was dark and full of potentially valuable canned goods, something else had probably gotten there first.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent, wry post-apocalyptic comedy that hits the brief: deliberation at home base, a mission for C-cells, escalating complications (Cult of the Checkout, Price-Check Badger, trolley escape), and a return home worse for wear. The Pratchett-esque flavor is attempted through footnote asides, deadpan narration, and the comic device of Chewy spouting corrupted advertising slogans ("Got milk?", "I'm lovin' it!", "Every kiss begins with Kay!"). The footnotes are a nice touch, though the first one ("collective will to pretend to know what a QR code was for") is the strongest joke in the piece. Strengths: The structure is tight and coherent; the world-building jokes (Temple of Mart, loyalty cards, un-scanned items as heresy) are genuinely funny and consistent; Chewy's malfunctioning slogans are a well-executed running gag with a good payoff at the end. The prose is clean and readable, with a consistent dry tone throughout. The ending lands well—Midas's resigned "Tomorrow would probably be worse" is appropriately wry. Weaknesses: The piece is more Pratchett-adjacent than Pratchett-quality. The humor is broad and the jokes are mostly one-note consumer-culture satire; the cultist dialogue is functional but flat, and the badger set-piece resolves too quickly and conveniently (a trolley conveniently nearby, a clean escape). Midas is thinly characterized beyond "hapless"—we're told about his knack for trouble rather than shown a distinctive personality. The emotional register is single-note: wry throughout, with little variation or depth. Some jokes overstay (the slogan gag is used four times, though the final one earns its place). The prose occasionally leans on stock phrasing ("a beacon of successful endeavour, a testament to human resilience"). The world-building, while amusing, is fairly predictable for the genre—ruined big-box stores as temples is well-trodden territory. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 74.3
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door didn’t so much jingle as shriek, a frantic, metallic clang that cut through the peaceful scent of old paper and brewing tea. A man stumbled in, slamming the door shut and pressing his back against it as if it were a besieged castle gate. He was breathing hard, a leather jacket scuffed at the elbows, dark hair a perfect, artful mess. He looked up, and Eira recognised him instantly from a billboard she’d seen on the one tedious trip to Cardiff last year. Julian Croft. The man whose face sold perfume and action figures to millions. He flashed a smile, a weapon of mass distraction that had probably toppled governments. "Apologies for the dramatic entrance. A bit of a… situation with the local wildlife." Eira didn't look up from the inventory list she was annotating. "We get a lot of seagulls in this part of the world. Vicious things when they want chips." There was a beat of silence. The smile wavered, just for a second. "Not seagulls, no. More like… piranhas with cameras." He pushed himself off the door, smoothing his jacket. His charm was a physical force, filling the small space of ‘The Last Page’. "This is a wonderful place. A real treasure. Charming." "It's dusty," Eira said, scratching a line through a miscounted ISBN. "And the roof leaks if you stand in the corner by the Welsh poetry." He chuckled, a low, practiced rumble. "Even more charming is its proprietor. I'm Julian, by the way." "Eira," she said, finally lifting her head. She let her gaze meet his for a fraction of a second before flicking back to her clipboard. "Did you need a book, Mr. Julian, or just a doorway?" He laughed again, but this time it was a little less certain. "Just Julian is fine. And I'm always in need of a good story." He leant against the counter, all casual grace. "You know who I am, of course." "Do I?" Eira tapped her pen on the clipboard. "Should I? You're not one of my late fee defaulters, are you?" His jaw tightened. The fragile ego, she thought, spotting the crack in the porcelain. "Julian Croft. The actor." "Right," Eira said, feigning a slow dawning of recognition. "Croft. Like the chap from that space film. The one with the exploding planets." Julian stared at her. The smile was completely gone now, replaced by a look of genuine, naked surprise. He was utterly derailed. "That was… Cillian Jones. And the planets didn't explode, they imploded. It’s a key narrative distinction." "Oh. My mistake." She went back to her list, but she could feel his eyes on her, no longer performing, just… looking. The energy in the room shifted. The pressure of his charm had vanished, replaced by something else, something curious and far more potent. He started pacing, a restless caged animal. His gaze fell on a small, cloth-bound display on the counter. He picked up a copy of *Fungi of the Welsh Coastline*. "An enthusiast," he said, his voice softer, the theatricality gone. "Someone has to be," Eira replied, her own voice losing a little of its sharp edge. "They don't catalogue themselves." He opened the book, his long fingers tracing the plate of a Fly Agaric. "My grandfather had a farm in the Cotswolds. He taught me. The thrill of the hunt. The quiet focus. You have to see the world differently, on your hands and knees in the dirt. It's… grounding." Eira looked up, really looked at him this time. He wasn't looking at her, but at the book, and for the first time, he looked less like a commodity and more like a person. A person who missed his grandfather. "It's the best time for it, after all this rain," she heard herself say. "The Ceps will be popping up under the beeches by the river." His head snapped up, his eyes alight with a genuine, unpolished excitement. "Ceps. You call them Ceps, not Porcini?" "They're Welsh," Eira said, a small smile touching her lips before she could stop it. "They have a proper name. Penny Buns, if you're feeling sentimental." "Penny Buns," he repeated, testing the words. The sound of it seemed to please him. "I haven't been foraging in years. Not a spot in London where you're not worried about picking up a discarded needle instead of a Morel." From outside, the sound of a car engine revving aggressively, followed by the squeal of tyres on wet tarmac. Then, silence. The threat was gone. The reason for his being here had vanished. Julian closed the book gently and placed it back on the counter. The space between them felt charged, thick with unspoken things. He didn't try to turn the charm back on. He just stood there, looking at her. "I suppose I should be going," he said, but he didn't move. "Right then," Eira said, her heart thumping a ridiculous, unprofessional rhythm against her ribs. He hesitated, then gestured vaguely towards the door. "They're not the only thing that’s popped up after the rain. The Chicken of the Woods… they like old oak, don't they? Down by the old mill, perhaps?" Eira felt a flush creep up her neck. He was asking. Not for her number, not for a date, but for a secret. For a piece of her world. "Maybe," she said, her voice barely a whisper. "But I don't show my best spots to just anyone, Mr. Croft." A slow, genuine smile spread across his face. It was nothing like the one he’d walked in with. This one was real. It didn't ask for anything, it just… was. "Julian," he corrected her softly. He held her gaze for a moment longer, then gave a small nod and slipped out the door, the bell giving a soft, final jingle. Eira stood perfectly still, staring at the closed door, until the scent of his expensive cologne was completely overpowered by the smell of rain and old books. She picked up the *Fungi of the Welsh Coastline*. Her fingers were trembling.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This scene executes the brief with notable skill. The premise (actor fleeing paparazzi into a Welsh bookstore) is delivered efficiently, and the dynamic requested — charm offensive derailed by the owner's immunity — plays out convincingly. Julian's fragile ego is shown through small tells: the wavering smile, the jaw tightening, the pedantic correction about imploding planets. Eira's deflections are dry and characterful ("late fee defaulters," "vicious things when they want chips"), and her internal softening is tracked through physical detail (the flush, the trembling fingers) rather than stated outright. The pivot device — the fungi book — is the scene's cleverest move. It gives Julian a genuine, non-performing self to reveal, and gives Eira a legitimate reason to lower her guard. The mushroom dialogue does double duty as flirtation ("I don't show my best spots to just anyone") without tipping into cliché. The ending, with the real smile replacing the professional one, lands the "unspoken chemistry" requirement with restraint. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally reaches for cleverness that misfires ("a weapon of mass distraction that had probably toppled governments" is a strained line; "piranhas with cameras" is serviceable but familiar). "The fragile ego, she thought, spotting the crack in the porcelain" is a rare moment of telling rather than showing, and it's oddly omniscient-adjacent in a scene otherwise anchored in Eira's POV. The paparazzi threat resolves a bit too neatly and conveniently — the engine revving and then silence, threat gone, purely functional. Some of Eira's rebuffs are slightly too scripted-quippy, edging toward rom-com banter rather than organic small-town reserve. The word count is well under the 1000-word seed, though the scene feels complete regardless. The Welsh setting is present but thin — a mention of Cardiff, Welsh poetry, rain, local naming conventions. It never feels falsely Welsh, but neither is it deeply rooted. The transformation of both characters is earned through the foraging exchange, which is the scene's greatest structural strength: the intimacy is built on shared knowledge rather than attraction, which makes the chemistry feel earned rather than asserted. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 78.4
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The great iron wheel of the door resisted for a moment, groaning like a beached leviathan, then turned with a sigh of pressurised air. The underhold of the Morska guild did not smell of dust and decay, but of the deep. A briny chill clung to the air, thick with the scent of whale oil, cold iron, and something else… the faint, ozone tang of immateria. The walls were not stone but the fossilised ribs of some impossibly ancient beast, arching over a floor of worn scrimshaw tiles that depicted a sunken city. Aya stepped inside, her bootheel clicking on the bone. The silence was a physical weight, pressing in on them. Behind her, Katra tensed, a hand straying to the weighted sap at her belt, while Simeon’s breath hitched, the frantic ticking of his pocket watch suddenly deafening in the stillness. *Too quiet,* Aya thought, her heart a frantic drum against her ribs. *Ambush.* The artefact they sought was said to be in a vault at the chamber’s heart, a Sycthan shard that could amplify a user’s connection to the immateria, turning a whisper into a scream. But there was no vault. No guards. No frantic looters taking advantage of the chaos. There was only a throne. It was a brutal construction of petrified jawbones and dark, oiled timber, and seated upon it was a woman they all knew. A woman who was supposed to be in a Piltovan gaol, her empire crumbling. Zofia. She was not the languid, perfumed courtier Aya had seen from afar. Dressed in practical, oil-stained leather, her dark hair was a tight, severe braid. A thin, white scar cut through one eyebrow, and her eyes, dark and sharp as obsidian shards, missed nothing. A harpoon gun lay across her lap, its trigger modified with a series of brass and copper fittings that hummed with a low, malevolent energy. Flanking her, two hulking brutes in canvas dusters and riveted goggles stood like silent, iron statues. Her krakens. “Lost, little rats?” Zofia’s voice was a purr of gravel and oil, devoid of any warmth. She hadn't moved, but her krakens had, shifting their weight to block the only exit. Katra snarled, a guttural sound of pure rage. “A trap.” “A lesson, you mean,” Zofia corrected, her gaze landing on Aya’s masked face. Aya felt it like a physical touch, a probing needle. “You think I wouldn’t smell ambition in my own house? You think a few coppers in the right pockets and a staged raid would be enough to unseat me?” She gestured vaguely with the harpoon gun. “The Watch are convenient idiots. They arrested my tailor. Poor man looked a bit like me from a distance.” Panic, cold and sharp, lanced through Aya. This wasn't a power vacuum; it was a spider’s web, and they had just stumbled into the centre. “Take them,” Zofia commanded, her voice flat. The krakens moved with terrifying speed. Katra managed to land a solid punch before a meaty fist sent her reeling. Simeon was simply grabbed, his spectacled face a mask of terrified resignation. Aya, her mind racing, tried to summon the whispers from the immateria, the dark entities that were her birthright, but the air was saturated with some kind of dampening field. The power sputtered and died within her. A rough hand seized her arm, spinning her around. Zofia rose from her throne, moving with a liquid, predatory grace. She reached out and, with a contemptuous flick of her wrist, ripped the mask from Aya’s face. The cheap silk fell away. In the gloom, illuminated by a single sputtering whale-oil lantern, Aya’s features were revealed: the high cheekbones of the Valerius line, the storm-grey eyes, the pale skin that had never known a day of hard labour. Katra and Simeon, now kneeling and brutally bound, stared at the floor. They had known, of course. They were her confidants. But the krakens grunted in surprise, and Zofia… Zofia smiled. It was a slow, terrible unfolding of her lips, a discovery far more satisfying than she had anticipated. “Well now,” the guild leader breathed, her voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. “What have we here? The little sparrow is a peacock in disguise.” She circled Aya, her eyes raking over her fine, if slightly dirty, clothes. “A Valerius. I’d recognise that inbred chin anywhere. Your father is Lord Alaric, is he not? The man who funds the Anti-Immateria Taskforce.” The irony was a gallows humour so bitter Aya almost laughed. Her world was collapsing, her two lives colliding with the force of a shipwreck. She saw it all: her father’s face, contorted not with anger, but with shame; the scandal that would destroy her family; the inevitable, public hanging that would reunite her with her mother. The ticking of Simeon’s watch marked each second of her impending doom. *Tick. My life is over.* *Tick. My name will be a curse.* *Tick. They will hang me.* “No,” Aya said, her voice shaking but finding a sliver of her aristocratic training. She forced herself to meet Zofia’s gaze. “You can’t kill us.” Zofia arched a scarred eyebrow. “Can’t I?” “My family,” Aya pressed on, the words tumbling out in a desperate rush. “They will pay. A king’s ransom. You’ll never have to steal again. You can buy a fleet, an island… anything. And if I disappear, they will turn this city upside down. The Guard, the army… they will burn the Morska guild to the ground to find me. I am more valuable to you alive than dead.” She was selling herself, bargaining for her life with the very name she had tried so hard to escape. The lies, the late nights, the thrill of the shadows—it all boiled down to this pathetic, sputtering plea. Zofia leaned in close, her breath smelling of salt and brass. “You think I care about coin, little noble? Gold is heavy. Power is light.” She tapped the side of Aya’s head with a gloved finger. “You have a spark in you. I felt it the moment you walked in. Your mother had it, too. A nasty little secret that got her neck stretched. They hanged her for the very thing you seek to wield.” Aya flinched as if struck. The deepest, most guarded part of her had just been laid bare. “You came here for the Sycthan shard,” Zofia continued, her voice a venomous caress. “You think it’s a key to power. It is. But not for you. Not yet.” She straightened up and looked down at them, a queen surveying her new, interesting pets. “You’re right about one thing. I’m not going to kill you. A hostage is useful. But not for ransom.” She turned to her krakens. “Take them below. Put the other two in the brine-pits. Let them think about their loyalty.” Her eyes locked onto Aya, a terrifying promise in their depths. “The little noblewoman and I are going to have a long talk about her mother’s magic. And you are going to learn to serve a new master.” The watch in Simeon’s waistcoat ticked on, a frantic, metal heart counting down the seconds to a fate far worse than death.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response is a strong execution of the prompt. It hits all required beats: the trio enters the underhold, confronts the un-incarcerated guild leader Zofia, are captured without a full fight scene, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates on her value as a hostage while grappling with exposure of her double life. The whalepunk/Victorian aesthetic is vividly rendered (fossilised ribs, scrimshaw tiles, whale-oil lanterns, harpoon gun with brass fittings), and the "men trust brass and oil" theme is woven in via the dampening field and Zofia's contempt for gold versus power. Dialogue is generally strong—Zofia's voice ("Gold is heavy. Power is light") is memorable, and Aya's internal monologue ("Tick. They will hang me.") is effective. Third person past tense is maintained. Weaknesses: the capture happens very quickly and with some convenience (the dampening field is a hand-wave to neutralise Aya's power). Katra and Simeon are thinly drawn, nearly voiceless—Katra gets one snarl, Simeon only his watch, which is a missed opportunity given the "authentic voices" instruction. Some phrases edge toward cliché ("predatory grace," "eyes dark and sharp as obsidian," "venomous caress"). The twist that the raid was staged is decent but the reveal is delivered via exposition monologue rather than dramatised. The ending's "fate worse than death" is slightly melodramatic, though tonally appropriate for gothic horror. Minor typos ("Sycthan" vs "scythan") mirror the prompt's inconsistency. Prose flows well overall; pacing is tight; the scene never meanders.
